To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

the beam system phase space density is related to the laboratory system charge density by the expression (2π)−3/2∑i=1N∫d3v′iδ3(r−r′i)δ(v−v′i−v0i)ρi(v′i) where N is the total number of particles in the beam, ri and vi are the particle position and velocity in the beam system, r′i and v′i are the particle position

the transformation of the phase space distributions between the beam and laboratory systems is given by the Jacobian of the transformation between the two sets of coordinates, with an additional factor of 1/2 to account for the fact that the beam system distribution is a probability density, while the laboratory system distribution is a charge density.

the transformation of the phase space densities from the laboratory to the beam system is given by the formula where the Jacobian of the transformation from the beam system to the laboratory system is given by The Jacobian is the determinant of the matrix of the partial derivatives of the transformation.
In summary, our research is concerned with
a self-consistent description of particle motion in a beam, and the self-fields generated by that motion.
the transformation of phase space densities in the two alternative descriptions, and with the transformation of particle motion equations in the two descriptions.
the transformation of phase space densities in self-consistent models of charged particle beams, and the application to coherent synchro-betatron oscillations.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that

the beam system phase space distribution function is the natural starting point for the self-consistent description of particle motion and fields in accelerators, but it is necessary to convert to the laboratory system to obtain the current density to be used in the Maxwell equations.

the transformation between the beam and the laboratory system descriptions of a beam is a linear integral operator, with a matrix kernel whose entries are the Bessel functions of the first kind, and that the transformation is invertible.

the beam system density is related to the laboratory system density in the following way: The beam system density is the laboratory system density, convoluted with the Jacobian of the transformation from the laboratory system to the beam system, and with a correction factor which depends on the Jacobian, the velocity distribution in the beam system, the beam size, and the beam current.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
we have developed a practical and rigorous method to describe the interaction of a particle beam with its own self-fields, in a way that can be applied to the study of a wide range of problems.
we have found a simple and practical way of expressing the beam charge/current density in the beam system coordinates as a function of the beam phase space density in those coordinates.
we have developed an exact and practical method for self-consistent simulation of the motion and radiation of a bunch of charged particles, in the presence of self-fields.
The main takeaway from our work is that
the beam system description is a powerful tool for self-consistent modeling, and the results can be used to transform the beam system density into the laboratory system density, and vice-versa.

the phase space density in the laboratory frame can be expressed in terms of the beam frame phase space density, but that the transformation formula is rather complicated, and it may be more convenient in practice to use the laboratory frame to solve the Maxwell equation, and to use the beam frame to follow particle motion.
the beam system description is a powerful and convenient tool in accelerator physics, even though it may seem to involve an unnecessary complication.
